best-mosquito-repellents-what-works-for-.title: Best Mosquito Repellents: What Works in a Mesa Backyard
best-mosquito-repellents-what-works-for-.content:
The best mosquito repellents are the ones that carry an EPA registration: DEET, picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus (or its synthetic form, PMD), IR3535 and 2-undecanone. Used on skin as the label directs, they give hours of protection, while candles, wristbands and ultrasonic gadgets do very little. If mosquitoes are still swarming your Mesa yard after you dump the water, call us at (480) 422-8388 or see our mosquito control in Mesa page.

Which Mosquito Repellents Actually Work?

Only the active ingredients that the EPA has evaluated for skin use have solid evidence behind them. The CDC points people to the same short list, and it is the list we tell Mesa homeowners to follow when they ask us what to buy at the store. The product name and the scent matter far less than the ingredient on the back of the bottle.

Active ingredientTypeHow it performsGood to know
DEETSyntheticLongest tested protection, rises with concentrationCan damage some plastics and synthetic fabrics
PicaridinSyntheticComparable to DEET at similar strengthNearly odorless and does not feel greasy
Oil of lemon eucalyptus / PMDPlant-basedGood protection, shorter than DEETThe EPA-registered form is not the same as plain lemon eucalyptus essential oil, and the label says not for children under three
IR3535SyntheticModerateGentle on skin, reapply more often
2-undecanonePlant-derivedModerateFound in some newer natural-style products

Is DEET safe to use on my family?

When used as directed, EPA-registered repellents are considered safe for adults and for children above the age on the label. Spray your hands and rub it on a child's face rather than spraying near the eyes and mouth, never put it under clothing or on cuts, and wash it off when you come inside. If you have questions about a baby or a pregnancy, ask your doctor.

Do natural repellents work as well?

Some do and many do not. Registered plant-based ingredients such as PMD hold up in testing, but a bottle of "essential oil blend" that has no EPA registration has not been tested the same way. Look for the EPA registration number on the label.

Which Mosquito Products Do Not Work?

Several popular products have little or no evidence behind them, and Mesa homeowners often buy them first because they sit by the register at the store. Skip these or treat them as a small extra:

  • Ultrasonic repellers and phone apps: studies have found they do not reduce bites.
  • Wristbands and clip-on devices: they protect only a tiny area around the band.
  • Vitamin B and garlic supplements: there is no reliable evidence that eating them keeps mosquitoes away.
  • Bug zappers: they kill mostly harmless insects, not the mosquitoes biting you.
  • Citronella candles: they add a small amount of smoke and scent, but they do not make a patio mosquito-free.

The same goes for backyard plants. We covered that in our post on plants that prevent mosquitoes, and the short version is that herbs help a little, not a lot.

How Long Does Each Repellent Last in Mesa Heat?

Less than the label suggests on a hot day. Sweat, swimming and a 105-degree afternoon all wear repellent off the skin faster, so reapply based on the label and use the heavier end of the protection range when you are outside for hours. In the cooler evenings of October through April, a single application tends to carry you much further.

What is the best way to apply it?

Put sunscreen on first, then repellent on top. Cover all exposed skin, including ankles and the backs of the neck and ears, which are the spots mosquitoes find first. Use only enough to cover the skin, and do not spray indoors in a closed room.

Can I treat my clothes too?

Yes. Permethrin is registered for treating clothing, shoes and camping gear, but never for use on skin. Treat items outdoors, let them dry fully, and follow the label.

Why Do Mosquitoes Bother Mesa Yards So Much?

Because Mesa is full of irrigated ground in a desert. Flood-irrigated lawns, canal laterals, neighborhood retention basins, and the green spaces around Riverview Park and Red Mountain keep water on the surface long after a monsoon storm has passed. Mosquitoes need only a bottle cap of water to breed, so a leaking drip valve in 85203 can feed a yard the same way a pond does.

Two groups cause most of the trouble. Culex mosquitoes breed in stagnant water and bite at dusk, while Aedes mosquitoes breed in small containers and bite in the daytime. Both can be active in Mesa from spring through the fall monsoon months, with the heaviest pressure from July through October. We talk more about that rhythm in our guide to stopping mosquitoes in the 85208 area of Mesa.

What Should You Do Around the House Besides Using Repellent?

Remove the water they breed in, because repellent protects only you while the mosquitoes keep multiplying a few feet away. A mosquito can go from egg to biting adult in about a week in Valley heat, so a once-a-week walk around the yard is the habit that makes the biggest difference. Check these spots first:

  1. Plant saucers, buckets, toys and anything else that holds water.
  2. Bird baths and pet bowls, which need scrubbing and refilling every few days.
  3. Drip irrigation valve boxes and low spots where water sits after watering.
  4. Gutters, rain barrels and the lids of covered containers after a storm.
  5. Swimming pools, fountains and spas that are no longer circulating.

Then add a layer of comfort. A fan on the patio does more than most people expect, because mosquitoes are weak fliers and have trouble reaching you in moving air. Sit away from dense shrubs and ivy, where mosquitoes rest in the shade during the day.

What should I do after I get bitten?

Wash the bite with soap and water and avoid scratching, since broken skin invites infection. A cold compress or an over-the-counter anti-itch product usually settles the itch. Mosquitoes in Arizona can carry West Nile virus, so let a doctor know if a fever, a severe headache or body aches follow a stretch of bites.

Does repellent matter in the cooler months?

Less, but it still counts. Mild Mesa evenings from October into November keep people outside and keep mosquitoes biting until the first real cold snap. Keep a bottle by the back door so it is there when you need it, and keep dumping standing water until the weather turns.

Repellent or Yard Treatment: Which Do You Need?

Repellent protects the person, and a yard treatment reduces the mosquitoes in the area. Most Mesa families end up using both during the worst months.

SituationBest approach
A hike, a ball game or a quick trip outsideEPA-registered repellent on skin
Occasional bites on the patioDump water weekly, run a fan, wear repellent at dusk
Bitten the moment you step outsideLook for hidden water, then call a professional
Daytime biting under shade treesA professional treatment of the resting areas
A neighbor's pool or a nearby basin is the sourceRepellent plus a professional yard treatment

A professional visit finds the breeding spots you cannot see, such as a covered valve box or a clogged drain, and treats the places where adult mosquitoes rest. If you are in Mesa, we cover neighborhoods across 85201 through 85215 and the surrounding East Valley.

Yes, and the mosquito picture is similar across the East Valley. See our mosquito pages for Gilbert, Chandler, Tempe and Queen Creek, or head to the pest control in Mesa overview for everything we handle. When you are ready, you can request service online.

  • Fruit flies and gnats helps if what you have are not true mosquitoes.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best mosquito repellent for kids?

Choose an EPA-registered product whose label allows use on children, such as picaridin or DEET at a moderate strength. Do not use oil of lemon eucalyptus on children under three, apply it to your own hands first, and keep it away from the eyes and mouth.

What is the best mosquito repellent for a patio or yard?

Repellent on skin works best for people, and a fan plus weekly water removal works best for the space. Spatial products like candles and coils give only a small area of relief, so do not rely on them for a whole yard.

How often should I reapply mosquito repellent in Arizona heat?

Follow the label, and reapply sooner if you are sweating heavily or have been in the pool. Heat and sweat shorten the protection time, especially in the summer months.

Do mosquito repellents work on Aedes mosquitoes that bite in the daytime?

Yes. EPA-registered repellents work on both Culex and Aedes mosquitoes, so use them whenever you are outside, not just at dusk.

Why do mosquitoes seem to bite me more than other people?

Mosquitoes follow carbon dioxide, body heat and skin chemistry, and those differ from person to person. That is why one person on the patio gets bitten while another is left alone, and why repellent matters even if you feel you are not a target.

can-cockroaches-fly-what-maricopa-homeow.title: Cockroaches That Can Fly: What Maricopa Homeowners Should Know
can-cockroaches-fly-what-maricopa-homeow.content:
Yes, some cockroaches can fly. In Maricopa the flyers are almost always American cockroaches, the big reddish-brown roaches many people call palmetto bugs, and smokybrown cockroaches. They fly short, clumsy distances when it is warm, when they are startled, or when they are drawn to a light. A flying roach in your house means they are getting in or breeding nearby.

Which Cockroaches Can Fly in Maricopa, AZ?

Most of the roaches people find indoors do not fly at all. German cockroaches have wings but almost never use them, and they tend to run for cover instead. The flyers we see around 85138 and 85139 come from two groups.

  • American cockroaches are the largest common house roach, usually 1.5 to 2 inches long, reddish brown with a pale yellowish band behind the head. They are the ones that glide through an open garage door at dusk.
  • Smokybrown cockroaches are slightly smaller, dark and glossy, and they are strong fliers that come to porch lights and patio lights at night.
  • Wood roaches and other outdoor species sometimes fly into homes near landscaping, especially at night, but they usually do not set up an indoor colony.

The common thread is size. Large winged roaches are outdoor and sewer-dwelling insects that wander inside, which is a different problem from the small German roach infestation that lives in a kitchen. If you want to compare, our Mesa guide to getting rid of German cockroaches covers the small kitchen roach.

How Do You Tell a Flying Roach From Other Flying Bugs?

A roach has a flat, oval body, long whip-like antennae and six spiny legs. Beetles and palo verde beetles in Maricopa look similar at a glance, but they have hard wing covers that meet in a straight line down the back and shorter antennae. Roaches have flatter, softer-looking wings that overlap.

InsectTypical sizeColorAntennaeWhere you usually see it
American cockroach1.5 to 2 inchesReddish brown with a light band behind the headLong, thinGarages, drains, block walls, patios at night
Smokybrown cockroach1 to 1.5 inchesDark glossy brownLong, thinAround lights, trees, roof edges
German cockroachAbout half an inchLight tan with two dark stripesLong, thinKitchens and bathrooms
Palo verde beetle2 to 3 inchesDark brown, hard shellShort, thickNear palo verde trees, summer evenings

Why Do Cockroaches Fly at Night in Maricopa?

Roaches fly when conditions favor it. Warm evenings, humidity after a monsoon storm and bright outdoor lighting all push American and smokybrown roaches to take off. They usually glide down from a wall or a tree rather than flying in a straight line, which is why one can seem to land on you out of nowhere.

Their flight is more of a controlled glide than steady flying. A roach will often launch from a wall, a tree trunk or a roofline and drift down toward the ground or the nearest light, then run for cover when it lands. In a neighborhood with block walls, mature landscaping and lit patios, there are plenty of launch points and plenty of places to land.

Does the heat make roaches fly more?

Warm weather makes them more active and more willing to fly. A long Arizona summer means that window runs for many months in Maricopa, and warm evenings can stretch into the fall.

Why do roaches come toward porch lights?

Smokybrown roaches in particular are drawn to light at night. A bright porch fixture near a door pulls them to the exact spot where they can slip inside when you open it.

Why Are Roaches Getting Into Maricopa Homes?

Maricopa is a young, fast-growing city, and many neighborhoods such as Rancho El Dorado, Province, Glennwilde, Tortosa and Cobblestone Farms sit on newer sewer lines, block walls and irrigated landscaping. Those are exactly the conditions American cockroaches prefer, because they live in sewers, storm drains and damp planter beds and come up to find food and water.

  • Sewer and drain access. We cover this in detail in our guide to sewer roaches in Maricopa.
  • Gaps around garage doors. A worn bottom seal is an open invitation for a large roach.
  • Irrigated landscaping. Damp mulch, leaf litter and thick groundcover give roaches shade and moisture right against the house, and overgrown beds are a harbor in the same way weeds are. Good weed and lawn care in Maricopa keeps these edges clean.
  • Block walls and wall voids. Roaches travel along the walls between yards, and the gaps at expansion joints and utility penetrations let them in.
  • Stored boxes and clutter. Cardboard in a garage gives them a place to hide during the day.

Is a Flying Cockroach a Sign of an Infestation?

It depends on how often it happens and where you see it. Timing matters: a roach in the garage after a monsoon storm is a different story from a roach on the kitchen counter at noon.

One flying roach on a hot night is not always an infestation, but it is a signal. If you see a single large roach once, it may have wandered in. If you see several in a week, or you see them in the daytime, they are living close to the house or inside it.

What does a roach infestation look like?

Look for droppings that resemble coffee grounds or black pepper, shed skins, egg cases and a musty smell. American cockroach egg cases are dark, bean-shaped capsules often found in hidden damp spots.

Are flying roaches dangerous?

They do not sting, but they walk through sewers, drains and garbage and then across your counters. Roaches are linked to allergy and asthma triggers, so get them under control rather than just swatting the ones you see. If you are wondering whether they can bite, read our guide on whether cockroaches bite.

How Do You Keep Flying Roaches Out of Your House?

You can cut down on roach entries. Do these first, and then bring in a professional for anything that keeps coming back.

  1. Replace worn garage door seals and weatherstrip exterior doors so there is no daylight at the bottom.
  2. Switch to yellow or warm LED bulbs near entry doors, or move bright lights away from the door itself, so they pull fewer night fliers to your threshold.
  3. Seal gaps around pipes, vents, cables and where block walls meet the slab.
  4. Cover floor drains and run water in rarely used sinks and tubs so the traps stay full.
  5. Pull mulch back a few inches from the foundation and clear leaf piles and wet debris near the house.
  6. Store boxes in plastic bins instead of cardboard in the garage.
  7. Fix leaks and wipe up standing water under sinks, because roaches need water more than food.

If you have a pool, a drip irrigation system or a lot of potted plants, you already have more moisture around the house than a typical desert yard, and that is worth checking first when roaches show up. Pool equipment pads, irrigation boxes and water meter boxes are common hiding spots close to the house.

Do Store-Bought Roach Sprays Work on Flying Roaches?

A spray kills the roach it touches and not much else. Large roaches live in sewers, wall voids and landscaping, so a can of spray on the kitchen floor does not reach the source. Repellent sprays can also push roaches deeper into walls, and a baited approach works better for the small species. For large outdoor roaches, treating the exterior perimeter and the entry points is what actually reduces how many reach your door.

We start with an inspection of the garage, the kitchen, the bathrooms, the exterior perimeter, the block walls and the landscaping. Then we treat the places where roaches enter and hide, tell you what to change around the home, and follow up to make sure the activity drops. Our roach elimination service in Maricopa is built around finding how they are getting in, not just treating what you can see. Roaches rarely come alone, and the same moisture and cracks that let one in can let other pests in too. Frequently Asked Questions

Can cockroaches really fly?

Yes. American and smokybrown cockroaches can fly, usually for short distances and mostly when it is warm. German cockroaches have wings but almost never fly.

Are palmetto bugs the same as cockroaches?

Yes. Palmetto bug is a nickname for a large cockroach, most often the American cockroach. They are the same insect.

It is most likely an American or smokybrown roach drawn to your lights on a warm night. It came from the sewer, a drain, landscaping or a block wall, so look for how it got in.

what-does-a-scorpion-sting-look-like-wha.title: What Does a Scorpion Sting Look Like? What Avondale Homeowners Should Know
what-does-a-scorpion-sting-look-like-wha.content:
A bark scorpion sting usually looks like very little: a tiny puncture or a faint pink spot, sometimes no mark at all. The sting is recognized by how it feels, with sharp burning pain, tingling and numbness that spread past the spot. If you were stung in Avondale and symptoms go beyond the sting site, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away.

This guide is general information about pests, not medical advice. For a sting that worries you, call Poison Control or a doctor, and call 911 for trouble breathing or swallowing.

What Does a Scorpion Sting Look Like on the Skin?

Most Arizona scorpion stings come from the bark scorpion, the small, pale tan scorpion that is common across the West Valley. Its venom works on the nerves, so the pain is out of proportion to what you can see. The skin often looks normal.

  • Little or no visible mark. You may see one tiny puncture, or nothing at all.
  • Mild redness or a small swollen spot. It is usually the size of a coin or smaller.
  • No big blister or spreading bruise. A sting that blisters, oozes or spreads in a widening red area is more likely a different bite, such as a spider or an infection setting in.

The better test is the feeling, not the look. Lightly tapping the area often makes the pain flare, a classic sign of a bark scorpion sting.

What Does a Scorpion Sting Feel Like?

Expect sudden, sharp, burning pain, like a hot needle. Within minutes you may feel pins and needles or numbness that moves up the arm, leg, foot or hand. Many people describe a strange "electric" feeling. The sting site may be sensitive to the touch of a sheet or a sock.

What you noticeTypical for a bark scorpion sting?What to do
Tiny puncture or no markYes, very commonWash the area and call Poison Control for guidance
Sharp burning pain, pain when tappedYesCool compress, keep the limb still, call Poison Control
Tingling or numbness near the stingYesWatch closely and call Poison Control
Numbness or tingling spreading far from the stingCan happenCall Poison Control or a doctor now

Large blister, spreading redness, pusNo, may be another bite or infectionSee a doctor

What Should You Do Right After a Scorpion Sting?

Stay calm and follow these steps. Poison Control in Arizona is free, staffed around the clock, and used to scorpion calls.

  1. Wash the sting site with soap and water.
  2. Apply a cool, damp cloth to the area. Do not put ice directly on the skin.
  3. Keep the stung arm or leg still and at about heart level.
  4. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and describe your symptoms.
  5. Take a photo of the scorpion if you can do it safely, or catch it in a jar, to confirm what stung you.

What should you not do after a scorpion sting?

Do not cut the skin, try to suck out venom, or use a tourniquet. None of it helps and some of it does harm. Do not put the stung limb in ice water, and do not give a small child any medicine until you have talked with Poison Control or a doctor. If the sting happened at night, do not just go back to sleep and hope it fades, because the symptoms you most need to catch can appear in the first hour or two.

Who should be seen quickly?

Young children, older adults and anyone with other health problems should be checked promptly. Children can have strong reactions, so do not wait to see if it passes.

How long does a scorpion sting last?

Pain and numbness commonly last for hours and can come and go for a day or more. A doctor or Poison Control can tell you what is normal for the person stung.

Why Are There Scorpions in Avondale, AZ?

Avondale sits on the Agua Fria River in the West Valley, with older neighborhoods around Historic Avondale and newer subdivisions across 85323 and 85392 such as Garden Lakes, Coldwater Springs and Rancho Santa Fe. Bark scorpions can live anywhere in that mix, and a few local features help them.

  • Block walls. Bark scorpions climb. They rest in the gaps and cap blocks of the walls between yards.
  • Irrigated landscaping. Damp mulch, rock beds and thick groundcover hold the insects scorpions eat, such as crickets and roaches.
  • River corridors and open desert edges. Land along the Agua Fria and the edge of the Estrella foothills sends scorpions toward new construction as it develops.
  • Stucco and door gaps. A scorpion can flatten itself to squeeze through a gap about the thickness of a credit card.

Scorpions are most active at night, mostly in the warm months, and they tend to be seen more after a monsoon storm drives them out of their hiding spots.

When are scorpions most active around Avondale homes?

Activity picks up as nights warm in spring and stays high through summer and into the fall. Evenings after the monsoon storms of July through September are a common time for a surprise sting, because the rain and humidity push scorpions and their prey out into the open. Most stings happen indoors at night: bare feet on a tile floor, a hand reaching into a shoe or a laundry pile, or a child rolling over onto one in bed.

How Do You Tell a Scorpion Sting From a Spider Bite?

A scorpion sting hurts immediately and sharply, with tingling and numbness. A spider bite is often painless at first and may show a red area, swelling or a blister hours later. If you saw the creature, a scorpion has pincers and a curled tail with a stinger. Our spider prevention in Avondale page covers the spiders people mix up with scorpions at the sting site.

How Do You Stop Scorpions From Getting Into an Avondale Home?

You will never remove every scorpion from the desert, but you can make your house a poor target.

Seal the entry points

Replace worn weatherstripping on the garage and entry doors, caulk gaps around pipes and cables, and close the gaps where block walls meet the house.

Cut off their food and shelter

Scorpions follow their prey. Controlling crickets, roaches and other bugs removes the reason they come near your walls. Move firewood, rock piles and stacked pots away from the house, and trim shrubs back from the stucco.

Check at night with a blacklight

Scorpions glow under a UV flashlight. A walk around the yard and block walls after dark shows you where they travel. Our technicians use the same blacklight method, then seal and treat the perimeter.

Shake it out

Shake out shoes, towels and clothes left on the floor or in the garage, and check bedding for kids who sleep near a wall.

Our scorpion control in Avondale program is built around finding how they get in. A technician walks the property, inspects with a blacklight, treats the perimeter and gaps, and works on the pests scorpions feed on. It is part of our Avondale pest and termite service for homes across Avondale. We have served Arizona homeowners since 2013.

Often like almost nothing. A bark scorpion sting may leave a tiny puncture or slight redness. Pain, tingling and numbness are the main signs.

Sometimes a small pink or red spot, but many stings leave no visible mark. A big blister or spreading redness points to something else.

When should I go to the ER for a scorpion sting?

Call 911 for trouble breathing or swallowing, drooling, or unusual eye or muscle movements. Children and older adults should be checked promptly, so call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 first.

how-to-get-rid-of-mice-in-the-house-what.title: How to Get Rid of Mice in the House: What Mesa Homeowners Should Do First
how-to-get-rid-of-mice-in-the-house-what.content:
To get rid of mice in a Mesa house, find and seal the gaps they use to get in, then trap the mice already inside with snap traps placed along walls. Traps alone never finish the job, because new mice keep coming through the same openings. If you hear scratching in your walls or attic, call us at (480) 422-8388 and our team will walk your property and show you the entry points.

We built this guide from what our technicians see in Mesa homes, from the older ranches near Dobson Ranch and Alta Mesa to newer stucco homes in Eastmark and Las Sendas. It covers how to confirm you have mice, what to do first, where they get in, and when it is time to bring in a pro. Our rodent exclusion in Mesa service follows the same order: inspect, seal, then remove.

How Do You Know You Have Mice in Your Mesa House?

The earliest signs are droppings, noises at night and chewed food packaging. Mouse droppings are small, dark and rice-shaped, usually found along baseboards, behind appliances and in pantry corners. Scratching or scurrying from walls or the attic, mostly after dark, is the other big clue.

  • Droppings. Fresh ones are dark and soft. Old ones are gray and crumble.
  • Gnawed packaging. Small, ragged holes in cereal boxes, pet food bags and bread.
  • Sounds. Light scratching, squeaks or running along walls, ceilings and under the sink.
  • Grease rub marks. Dark smudges along walls where mice run the same path every night.
  • A musty, ammonia-like smell in closets, the garage or the pantry.
  • Nests. Shredded paper, fabric or insulation tucked behind storage boxes.

Mice rarely show themselves in daylight. If you see one in the open during the day, the population is usually larger than you think.

Is It a Mouse, a Roof Rat or a Pack Rat?

Treatment depends on what is actually in your house, and Mesa has more than one rodent. House mice are the small ones that stay low. Roof rats climb, so they get into attics, palm trees and block walls. Droppings size is the fastest field test.

What you findLikely rodentWhere it shows up in Mesa
Rice-sized droppings, scattered by the dozens, gnawed foodHouse mouseKitchens, pantries, garages, behind appliances
Larger, capsule-shaped droppings, noise overhead, gnawed fruitRoof ratAttics, citrus and palm trees, tops of block walls
Piles of sticks, cactus joints and debris, chewed wires in a vehiclePack ratDesert lots, rock yards, edges near Usery Mountain
Tiny droppings plus greasy trails along baseboardsHouse mouseOlder homes, rentals, apartments with shared walls

If the droppings are bigger than a grain of rice, you may be dealing with a rat rather than a mouse. That is a different job, and our guide to rodent-proofing a Mesa home in Eastmark covers the larger species.

How Do Mice Get Into a House in Mesa?

Mice squeeze through any gap about the size of a dime. Mesa homes give them a lot of options, and almost all are at ground level or at the roof edge. Walk the outside of your home slowly and look at each of these.

Garage door and side-door gaps

A worn rubber seal at the bottom of a garage door is the number one entry point we find. If you can see daylight under the door, a mouse can get through. Check weatherstripping on side doors as well.

Where lines and cables enter the wall

Look at the spots where cable, gas and pipe lines pass through stucco or block. Builders often leave a ring of open space around them. A gap you can fit a pencil into is big enough.

Roof edges, tile and vents

Barrel-tile roofs leave small openings under the first row of tiles, and attic vents without a screen are an easy way in. Roof rats favor these routes, and mice follow them if the openings are low.

Block walls, citrus and palms

A trimmed tree touching the roofline gives rodents a bridge. Fruit that falls and stays on the ground draws them to the yard in the first place.

What Should You Do First to Get Rid of Mice?

Start by removing what feeds them and finding where they travel, before you set a single trap. This order matters because mice are cautious and learn the layout of a space quickly. Here is the sequence we recommend.

  1. Put food away. Move pet food, cereal and bread into hard plastic or glass containers with tight lids.
  2. Clean up. Sweep crumbs, wipe counters and take out the trash every night until the problem is solved.
  3. Map the activity. Look for droppings and rub marks to see where mice run, then set traps there.
  4. Seal the obvious gaps. Steel wool packed into a hole, then topped with caulk or patch material, holds up better than foam alone because mice chew foam.
  5. Set snap traps. Place them against walls, with the trigger end facing the wall, since mice hug walls as they travel.
  6. Check traps daily and wear gloves when disposing of mice.

What is the best bait for mouse traps?

A pea-sized dab of peanut butter works well, pushed firmly into the trigger. Mice lick it off rather than grab and run, which sets the trap off. Chocolate and a bit of nesting material such as cotton work too.

Do Home Remedies and Poison Actually Work?

Peppermint oil, ultrasonic plug-ins and mothballs will not clear a real infestation. Mice may avoid a spot for a day or two, then return. We also do not recommend loose poison bait around a house. A mouse that eats it can die inside a wall, where the smell lasts for days, and pets and wildlife can be exposed.

Mesa mice are active all year, but pressure builds in late fall and winter. When nights drop into the 40s, mice look for warm, dry shelter, and a garage or attic fills the need. Summer heat, which regularly passes 100 degrees, also drives them indoors to the shade of walls and pantries.

Why Does Sealing Matter More Than Trapping?

Trapping removes the mice you have now. Sealing stops the next group. A single female mouse can have several litters a year, so a handful of unsealed gaps can refill your house within weeks. This is why a trap-only approach feels like it works for a week and then stops.

Yes. Insects bring more than their own trouble. Roaches and other bugs give mice a steady food source, and pests like these draw in scorpions, which hunt in the same dark corners. A black widow bite often looks like very little: a tiny red spot, sometimes two faint puncture marks, with mild swelling and a bit of redness around it. What makes it serious is how you feel, not how it looks. Cramping, sweating or a rigid belly within a few hours means you should get medical care right away. What Does a Black Widow Spider Bite Look Like?

A widow bite is usually a small, pale or reddish spot, sometimes with two tiny marks, and a ring of mild redness or swelling. Many people feel only a pinprick, and some do not notice it at all. The skin rarely tells the full story, so the first hour matters most.

  • The mark. One or two tiny puncture points, often hard to see without a close look.
  • The skin around it. Mild redness, a small raised area, or a faint target-like ring in some cases.
  • The feeling. A sharp pinprick at first, followed by a dull, spreading ache.
  • What comes next. Pain that moves toward the chest or belly, muscle cramps, sweating, nausea or a rigid stomach, usually within one to three hours.

Not every bite delivers venom, and many are mild. Still, the symptoms that follow are what separate a widow bite from a harmless one, so do not wait for the mark to "look bad."

How Can You Tell a Black Widow Bite From Other Bites?

The mark alone cannot tell you, so look at what else is going on. Mosquito and bed bug bites itch. Scorpion stings burn right away. Widow bites tend to look quiet on the skin and then cause body-wide muscle pain. This table shows the pattern we hear about most from Phoenix homeowners.

What Should You Do If a Black Widow Bites You?

Wash the bite with soap and water, apply a cold pack and call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. That number works anywhere in Arizona and connects you with a specialist at any hour. If you have severe pain, cramping, trouble breathing or a stiff belly, call 911 or go to an emergency room.

  2. Clean the bite with soap and water.
  3. Cool it. A cold pack wrapped in a cloth for short stretches eases the pain.
  4. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or seek emergency care for symptoms beyond the bite itself.
  5. If you can, safely save the spider in a jar or take a photo. It helps with identification.

Children, older adults and anyone with a heart condition or high blood pressure should be seen sooner rather than later. Treat this section as general safety information, not medical advice, and follow what your doctor or Poison Control tells you.

How Do You Know It Is a Black Widow and Not Another Spider?

Look for a shiny, jet-black body with a red hourglass marking on the underside of the abdomen. Females are the ones that matter, since they are the larger spiders and the ones people usually run into. The web is the second clue: it is a messy, tangled web of thick, strong silk that you feel resist if you brush it.

Males and young spiders look different. They are smaller, with lighter coloring and stripes, which is why a Phoenix homeowner sometimes thinks they have found a "different" spider. If you are not sure, a photo sent to us is the quickest way to find out. You will see more detail in our post on whether black widows can kill you and where they hide in Mesa.

Where Do Black Widows Hide Around Phoenix Homes?

Widows go where it is dark, dry and left alone. In Phoenix that means the places you reach into without looking, plus the spots that stay shaded when the day tops 100 degrees.

Meter boxes, valve covers and pool equipment

Water meter boxes and irrigation valve covers are among the first places our technicians check. They stay cool, they hold insects and a widow can build a web under the lid in a few days. Pool pump housings and equipment pads work the same way.

Block walls, woodpiles and stacked pots

The bottom edge of a block wall, stacked clay pots, firewood and old lumber all give a widow cover. Reach into these with gloves, never bare hands.

Garages and storage

Cardboard boxes, shelving corners and the area behind a water heater are common garage hiding places. Widows prefer a quiet corner near the floor, so they are rarely in the middle of a room.

Patio furniture and grill covers

Underneath chair rims and inside grill covers are favorites. Check before you sit, especially if the furniture has been in one spot for a while.

Why Are Black Widows Common in Phoenix Neighborhoods?

Widows follow their food, which is other insects, and Phoenix has plenty. Porch lights draw moths and beetles at night, irrigated landscaping holds crickets, and block walls and rock yards give widows shelter that stays shaded from the summer sun. That mix of food and cover is why they turn up in 85050 and 85054 near Desert Ridge as readily as in 85024 and 85023 around Deer Valley and Moon Valley.

That also means a widow problem rarely stands alone. Reducing the other insects reduces the food supply, a point we cover in why spiders love Phoenix homes. If your yard also draws scorpions, they follow the same insects, and our scorpion control in Phoenix work covers both.

How Do You Keep Black Widows Away From Your Home?

Remove the clutter they live in, seal the gaps they use and cut down the insects they eat. You will not get to zero by yourself, but these steps make a big difference.

  • Wear gloves when you move boxes, wood, pots or anything stored outside.
  • Keep woodpiles and stacked items off the wall and away from the house.
  • Swap white outdoor bulbs for warm-toned ones, which draw fewer night insects.
  • Knock down webs with a long-handled brush or vacuum, and check the same spots again a week later.
  • Seal gaps around doors, garage doors and utility lines.
  • Shake out gloves, shoes and towels that sat outside.

The web is the part DIY sprays tend to miss. Our technicians treat the web sites and the perimeter, then come back to the same hiding spots. are-scorpions-arachnids-what-queen-creek.content:
Yes, scorpions are arachnids, not insects. They are in the same class as spiders, ticks and mites, with eight legs, two main body sections and no antennae or wings. That difference matters in Queen Creek, because the sprays and sticky traps made for insects often miss scorpions entirely. If you are finding scorpions around your home, call us at (480) 422-8388.

Are Scorpions Arachnids or Insects?

Scorpions are arachnids. Insects have six legs, three body sections and usually antennae and wings. Arachnids have eight legs, two body sections and no antennae. A scorpion fits the arachnid pattern on every point, along with a pair of pincers and a tail that curls over its back.

The scientific order is Scorpiones, and scorpions are one of the oldest land animals on earth, dating back hundreds of millions of years. Here in the Sonoran Desert, they are a normal part of the landscape. The trouble starts when they follow food and shade into our homes.

  • Eight legs. Four on each side, which is the quickest way to rule out an insect.
  • Two body sections. A front section that holds the head and legs, and a segmented abdomen that ends in the tail.
  • Pincers. The pedipalps look like small claws and are used to grab prey.
  • No wings, no antennae. Insects such as roaches and crickets have antennae. Scorpions do not.

How Can You Tell a Scorpion From an Insect or Another Arachnid?

Count the legs, then look for the tail and claws. A scorpion is the only common Arizona arachnid with both a curled, stinger-tipped tail and pincers. Spiders and solifugids ("sun spiders") are arachnids too, but they lack the tail.

What Kind of Scorpion Lives in Queen Creek?

The Arizona bark scorpion is the one you will meet in Queen Creek. It is small, about two to three inches long, pale yellow-tan, and slender. It is also the most venomous scorpion in North America, so it is the one worth taking seriously, especially around young children.

Bark scorpions climb. They scale stucco, block walls and tree trunks, and they can hang upside down from a ceiling. That is why people find them in sinks, bathtubs and light fixtures. Giant hairy scorpions live in Arizona too, but they stay on the ground and are rarely found in houses.

Why does the arachnid label matter for control?

Scorpions behave nothing like the insects most sprays are made for. They do not groom and swallow residue the way roaches and ants do, and they spend much of the day tucked in cracks, under rocks and inside wall voids. Because they hunt other pests, the food supply and the hiding places both have to be dealt with, not just the scorpion you see.

Do Scorpions Glow Under a Black Light?

Yes. Scorpions glow a bright blue-green under ultraviolet light, which is how our technicians find them after dark. Their outer shell contains compounds that fluoresce, so a UV flashlight turns a dark yard into a clear map of where they are.

You can do a simple check on your own. Wait until an hour or two after sunset, shine a UV flashlight along block walls, around the base of the house, along rock beds and near any water source, and note where you see a glow. Bring that list to us, since it shows us where to focus.

Why Are Scorpions So Common Around Queen Creek Homes?

Queen Creek sits at the edge of the desert and next to farmland, and both help scorpions. New construction on the east side along Ellsworth Road and out toward Hastings Farms and Sossaman Farms turns up soil that scorpions have lived in for years. The washes, irrigation lines and orchard edges near Schnepf Farms add moisture and the insects scorpions eat.

  • Irrigation and pet water. Moisture draws crickets and roaches, which scorpions hunt.
  • Gaps at the house. Weatherstripping, garage door seals and utility penetrations let small scorpions in.

That is why a clean, well-kept home can still have them. Our post on scorpion control for Hastings Farms homeowners covers more about the east side of town.

How Do You Keep Scorpions Out of Your House?

Close the gaps, reduce the food and clear out the hiding spots. A scorpion that cannot get in, and finds nothing to eat, moves on. None of these steps work alone, but together they cut sightings.

  1. Seal entry points. Replace worn door sweeps, caulk gaps around pipes and cables, and check garage door seals.
  2. Cut back vegetation. Trim branches that touch the roof or walls, since bark scorpions climb them.
  3. Move woodpiles and rocks away from the house, and lift stored items off the garage floor.
  4. Control the insects. Fewer crickets and roaches means less to hunt.
  5. Shake out shoes and towels that sat on the floor or outside.

Wash the area with soap and water, apply a cool compress and call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. A bark scorpion sting burns at once and can cause numbness or tingling. Call 911 for trouble breathing, muscle twitching or any reaction in a young child or older adult. how-do-scorpions-breed-what-mesa-homeown.title: How Do Scorpions Breed? A Mesa Homeowner Guide to Bark Scorpion Babies
how-do-scorpions-breed-what-mesa-homeown.excerpt: Scorpions mate in a courtship dance and give birth to live young. Here is how bark scorpions breed, how fast babies grow, and how to stop them in Mesa.
how-do-scorpions-breed-what-mesa-homeown.content:
Bark scorpions mate in a slow courtship dance, carry their young for several months and give birth to live babies, usually a dozen or more at a time. The newborns are pale, about the size of a grain of rice, and ride on their mother's back for roughly their first week. For Mesa homeowners, that means one scorpion in the garage can turn into a family if the hiding places and the food stay put. If you are seeing small scorpions, call us at (480) 422-8388.

We get this question most often from families in 85207, 85209 and 85212 who found a tiny scorpion and wondered where it came from. This guide walks through how scorpions find a mate, how the babies are born, how long they take to grow up, and what all of it means for scorpion control around a Mesa home. Our scorpion control in Mesa service is built around breaking that cycle.

How Do Scorpions Breed?

Scorpions breed through a courtship dance. The male grabs the female's pincers and walks her back and forth until he finds a flat spot. He then deposits a packet of sperm on the ground and guides her over it. Fertilization happens inside the female, not in an egg that she lays.

The dance can last anywhere from a few minutes to several hours. Scorpion experts call it the promenade à deux. It tends to happen at night during the warm months, when scorpions are most active, which is why you may never see it even if it happens a few feet from your patio.

  • Courtship. The pair locks pincers and the male leads the female in a slow back-and-forth walk.
  • Sperm transfer. The male leaves a sperm packet on the ground and positions the female over it.
  • Separation. Afterward the pair parts. Males often leave quickly, because a female may treat a male as food.

Do Scorpions Lay Eggs or Give Birth to Live Young?

Scorpions give birth to live young. The Arizona bark scorpion carries its developing embryos inside the body and delivers fully formed babies, called scorplings. It does not lay eggs in a nest the way spiders and insects do. That is one reason there is no egg sac for you to find and remove.

Pregnancy takes several months, and the exact length depends on temperature and species. A litter of bark scorpions is commonly in the range of a dozen to a few dozen babies. Giant hairy scorpions, the larger Arizona species, have smaller families and almost never live inside homes.

What Happens to Baby Scorpions After They Are Born?

Newborns climb onto their mother's back and stay there while their first shell hardens. They are soft and nearly white, and they do not feed during this stage. After their first molt, which usually comes within about one to two weeks, they drop off and begin hunting on their own.

From there, young scorpions shed their outer shell several more times as they grow. Each molt leaves them softer and more vulnerable for a day or so, so they hide in cracks and tight spaces. The whole trip to adulthood commonly takes a year or longer, and bark scorpions can live for several years once they are grown.

Baby scorpions show up most often during the warm months, roughly spring through early fall, when mating and birth both pick up. That lines up with the summer monsoon, when humidity rises, insects increase and scorpions move around more. You can still find them in cooler months, because scorpions slow down rather than disappear.

A single sighting of a small, pale scorpion is worth taking seriously, since it tells you adults are probably nearby.

Why Do Scorpions Keep Coming Back to the Same Yard?

Scorpions return to places that give them food, shade and a safe spot to raise young. Bark scorpions also tolerate each other better than most species, so they gather in groups in the same cracks and voids. A good spot gets reused year after year.

  • Food. Crickets, roaches and other small insects draw them. Our guide on what scorpions eat in Mesa goes through what pulls them in.
  • Shelter. Gaps in block walls, loose stucco, stacked pots and landscape rock all work as nurseries.
  • Moisture. Irrigation lines, pet bowls and drip emitters bring prey and cool the ground.
  • Entry points. Worn door sweeps, garage seals and pipe penetrations let juveniles slip inside.

How Can You Tell If Scorpions Are Breeding on Your Property?

The clearest sign is seeing juveniles, or an adult carrying babies. Other signs are several sightings in the same spot over a few weeks, or scorpions of different sizes in one area. If you see any of them, there is probably a population nearby, not a lone wanderer.

A UV flashlight is the easiest tool to check. Scorpions glow blue-green under ultraviolet light, including the small ones. After dark, scan block walls, the base of the house, rock beds and the garage, and write down where you see a glow. Our guide to whether scorpions are arachnids explains why they fluoresce.

How Do You Stop Scorpions From Multiplying Around Your Mesa Home?

Take away the shelter and the food, and close the gaps they use to get indoors. This does not remove every scorpion, but it makes your property a poor place to raise young. We recommend doing it alongside a professional treatment.

  1. Clear out the hiding places. Move wood, pavers, pots and clutter away from the foundation and off the garage floor.
  2. Seal the house. Replace door sweeps, caulk gaps around pipes and cables, and check weatherstripping.
  3. Trim plants. Cut back branches that touch the roof or walls, since bark scorpions climb.
  4. Cut the food supply. Managing crickets and roaches leaves them less to hunt.
  5. Check at night with UV. Repeat every few weeks in warm months to see if the numbers are dropping.

What Are Sugar Ants and Why Are They in My Scottsdale Kitchen?

"Sugar ant" is a nickname, not one species. In Scottsdale it usually means a small, sweet-loving ant such as the Argentine ant, the odorous house ant or the Forelius ant, all of which follow scent trails to syrup, fruit, pet food and anything greasy or sticky. They come inside because your kitchen is a reliable buffet and, in summer, a reliable source of water.

Scottsdale's landscaping makes it easy for them. Lawns, drip irrigation, citrus trees and mature oleander in neighborhoods like McCormick Ranch and Gainey Ranch keep soil damp, and damp soil means ant colonies that stay active all year. When a hot afternoon dries the yard, those same ants send foragers into the house looking for moisture.

How Do You Repel Sugar Ants Without a Pest Company?

The most effective do-it-yourself method is to break the scent trail, remove the food and block the doorway. Ants lay a chemical path that other ants follow, so wiping it away confuses the line for a while. That only helps if you also take away what they came for.

  1. Follow the trail to its start. Watch the line for ten minutes. Note where it enters, usually a window track, a gap near a pipe or a crack at the baseboard.
  2. Wipe the trail clean. Use soapy water or a vinegar and water mix on the whole path, not only the part you can see on the counter.
  3. Seal food in hard containers. Honey, syrup, sugar, cereal, pet food and fruit bowls should not sit open overnight.
  4. Rinse and dry. Rinse jars and cans before recycling, and dry the sink and counters before bed.
  5. Close the entry. Caulk small gaps, repair door sweeps and tighten the seal around pipes.
  6. Move the outside pressure away. Trim branches touching the roof or walls and keep mulch a hand's width off the foundation.

Those steps work best as prevention. Once you have a steady trail, the ants you see are only a small part of the colony.

Which Home Remedies Actually Repel Ants, and Which Don't?

They come back because the colony is still alive and the trail has simply been rebuilt. A wiped trail is a setback of a few hours, not a defeat. Foragers keep scouting, find the food again and re-lay the scent.

  • The water never stops. A leaking hose bib, an overwatered bed or a damp spot under a sink keeps foragers coming even when the kitchen is clean.
  • There are multiple entry points. Closing one gap pushes the trail to the next one.

If your kitchen trail returns every few days, that is the sign that the problem is bigger than a cleaning routine.

Are Sugar Ants Harmful, or Just Annoying?

Sugar ants do not sting in any way that matters and they do not damage wood, so they are mostly a nuisance. The real concern is hygiene. Ants that walk through trash and drains and then across your counters can spread bacteria onto food prep areas, and a big colony can make a kitchen very hard to use.

The bigger risk is mistaking a different ant for a sugar ant. Carpenter ants can damage wood, and fire ants sting. best-grass-lawn-fertilizer-what-scottsda.excerpt: The best lawn fertilizer in Scottsdale is a slow-release, nitrogen-led feed matched to the season and your grass. Here is what to buy, when to apply it and when to call us.
best-grass-lawn-fertilizer-what-scottsda.content:
The best grass lawn fertilizer for Scottsdale is a slow-release, nitrogen-led product applied in the right season for your grass: a high-nitrogen feed with iron for Bermuda from spring through early fall, and a light starter feed for winter ryegrass. Buying the "best" bag matters less than timing and soil. If your lawn is yellow, patchy or thin, call us at (480) 422-8388 and we will build a schedule through our lawn fertilization in Scottsdale service.

We get this question from homeowners in 85251, 85254, 85258, 85260 and 85262, and the honest answer starts with a different question: which grass do you have, and what month is it? A fertilizer that greens up a Bermuda lawn in June can do almost nothing in January, and the wrong bag at the wrong time can feed weeds instead of turf.

What Is the Best Fertilizer for a Scottsdale Lawn?

For most Scottsdale lawns, the best fertilizer is a slow-release nitrogen fertilizer with added iron, applied during the growing season. Nitrogen drives leaf growth and color, slow-release forms feed steadily instead of burning the lawn, and iron fixes the yellowing common in our alkaline desert soil.

Here is what that means in practice:

  • Nitrogen leads. Nitrogen is the first number on the bag and the nutrient turf uses most.
  • Slow-release beats quick-release. Slow-release pellets spread the feeding over weeks. Quick-release products give a fast flush, but they are easier to overdo in summer heat.
  • Iron helps desert lawns. Our soil pH is high, which can lock up iron. A yellow lawn with green veins in the blades is a classic sign.
  • Read the label for your grass. A product for cool-season lawns is not a match for Bermuda in July.

What Do the Three Numbers on a Fertilizer Bag Mean?

The three numbers are the percentage of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) in the bag, always in that order. A 20-5-10 product, for example, is 20 percent nitrogen, 5 percent phosphorus and 10 percent potassium. Turf needs the most nitrogen, so a lawn feed usually has a high first number.

NumberNutrientWhat it does for turfScottsdale note
First (N)NitrogenLeaf growth and green colorThe main nutrient to apply on a schedule
Second (P)PhosphorusRoot development, mostly for new seedOften already adequate in desert soil, so a soil test beats guessing
Third (K)PotassiumStress, heat and drought toleranceUseful going into summer
ExtraIronDeeper green, fixes chlorosisOften the simplest fix for a pale lawn in alkaline soil

Phosphorus is the one most homeowners over-apply. Many Valley soils already hold plenty, so we recommend a soil test before you add more.

Should You Fertilize Bermuda and Winter Rye Differently?

Yes. Bermuda is a warm-season grass that grows hard from spring to early fall and goes dormant in winter, so we feed it when it is growing. Perennial ryegrass, which many Scottsdale homeowners overseed in October for green winter turf, is a cool-season grass and needs a lighter feed through the cooler months.

That split is why a single "lawn fertilizer" answer fails here. Treating dormant Bermuda like it is in July wastes product, and skipping the ryegrass feed leaves the winter lawn pale and thin.

When Should You Fertilize a Lawn in Scottsdale? A Season-by-Season Guide

Feed Bermuda from roughly April through September once it has fully greened up, and feed overseeded ryegrass lightly through the winter. Spring warmth, not the calendar date, is the real trigger: wait until Bermuda is growing, not just waking up.

If you are reading this in early November, your ryegrass should already be up. A light feeding now keeps it dark green, and we would hold off on any Bermuda feeding until spring.

Can Fertilizer and Weed Control Be Applied at the Same Time?

Sometimes, but not always. A "weed and feed" product combines fertilizer with a herbicide. A pre-emergent in that mix can stop grass seed from sprouting, so it can undo an overseeding job. Plan weed prevention and feeding as two separate steps and put each in the right season.

We lay out how we sequence these on our pre-emergent weed control in Scottsdale page. If you want a winter lawn, our guide to overseeding timing near Grayhawk explains why the order matters.

Why Is My Scottsdale Lawn Yellow Even Though I Fertilize?

A lawn that stays yellow after feeding usually has an iron or watering problem, not a nitrogen problem. High pH can keep iron out of reach, overwatering washes nutrients below the roots, and shallow, frequent watering builds up salts at the surface. More nitrogen will not fix any of those.

  • Yellow with green veins: often iron chlorosis in alkaline soil.
  • Pale all over in summer: usually not enough nitrogen, or nitrogen that leached out after heavy watering.
  • Brown, crunchy patches after feeding: fertilizer burn from too much product or no water afterward.
  • Thin lawn with weeds taking over: a feeding problem and a weed problem together, and weeds often win in thin turf.

If weeds are part of what you are seeing, our Bermuda grass guide for McCormick Ranch covers one of the most common culprits in Scottsdale yards.

How Much Fertilizer Should You Use?

Follow the bag label for your grass and your lawn size, and do not guess. A common rule of thumb for turf is about one pound of actual nitrogen per 1,000 square feet per feeding, but the label is the final word because products differ in strength. Measure the lawn, set the spreader to the label setting and water the lawn afterward.

Many Scottsdale properties have smaller turf areas next to rock and desert landscaping, so measuring matters. Spreading a full-lawn dose over a small patch is the easiest way to burn grass. Our Scottsdale lawn nutrition guide near the McDowell Sonoran Preserve goes through how we think about feeding turf next to desert edges.

DIY Fertilizer or Professional Lawn Fertilization?

DIY works well for a small, healthy lawn and a homeowner who will read labels and keep a schedule. A professional visit makes more sense when the lawn is large, the color is uneven, weeds keep returning or you are juggling overseeding and weed control together.

  1. We look at the lawn first. We identify the grass, check the thatch and moisture, and note any weed pressure.
  2. We match the product to the season. That means the right feed for Bermuda in summer and the right one for ryegrass in winter.
  3. We keep weed control and feeding in order. That avoids the overseeding conflict described above.
  4. We tell you what to change. Watering depth, mowing height and timing matter as much as the product.

how-to-get-rid-of-wood-boring-bees-what-.title: How to Get Rid of Wood-Boring Bees: What Tempe Homeowners Should Know About Carpenter Bees
how-to-get-rid-of-wood-boring-bees-what-.excerpt: Wood-boring bees in Tempe are almost always carpenter bees. Here is how to confirm them, what they damage, what actually stops them and when to call us.
how-to-get-rid-of-wood-boring-bees-what-.content:
To get rid of wood-boring bees in Tempe, first confirm they are carpenter bees by looking for round, half-inch holes in bare wood with sawdust underneath, then treat the gallery, plug the hole after the bees are gone and paint or stain the wood so they do not return. They do not eat wood, but a nest reused for years can weaken fascia, rafters and pergola beams. If you would rather not work from a ladder near a nest, call us at (480) 422-8388 and we will inspect it through our bee and wasp removal in Tempe service.

We hear this question from homeowners across 85281, 85282, 85283 and 85284, from the older ranch homes near Mill Avenue and Tempe Town Lake to the newer patios and pergolas on the south side near Papago Park. The pattern is the same everywhere: a big, shiny, bumble-bee-looking insect hovers near the eaves in spring, and a few weeks later there is a tidy round hole and a little pile of sawdust on the patio table.

What Are Wood-Boring Bees in Arizona?

Wood-boring bees are carpenter bees: large, solitary bees that chew a tunnel into dry wood to raise their young. In the Phoenix metro the Valley carpenter bee is the one most homeowners see. Unlike termites, they do not eat the wood. They chew it out, push the sawdust away and lay eggs in side chambers.

A few facts help you tell them apart from other bees:

  • Size and look. Carpenter bees are large and robust, often about an inch long. Females are typically dark and shiny, and males in our area are often golden-brown and fuzzy.
  • Bare abdomen. A bumble bee has a fuzzy, hairy back end. A carpenter bee usually has a smooth, shiny one.
  • Solitary habits. There is no big colony or paper nest. Each female digs her own tunnel, though several may use the same stretch of wood.
  • Hovering males. Males guard the nest area and dart at anything that moves. They have no stinger, so the dive-bombing is mostly bluff.

How Do You Know It Is a Carpenter Bee and Not Termites or Honey Bees?

Look at the hole and the debris. A carpenter bee entrance is a clean, perfectly round hole about half an inch across, usually on the underside or face of bare wood, with coarse, sawdust-like frass below it. Termites leave mud tubes or tiny pellets, and honey bees live in a wax comb inside a wall or tree cavity, not in a drilled tunnel.

SignCarpenter beeTermitesHoney bees
Entry pointRound hole, about 1/2 inch, drilled into bare woodNo clean hole; mud tubes or tiny pinholesGap or crack in a wall, soffit or tree
DebrisCoarse sawdust and yellow-brown streaks below the holeSmall pellets or discarded wingsWax, honey stains, bees in a steady stream
SoundFaint chewing or buzzing in the woodQuiet, or soft clicking in wallsLoud steady hum inside a wall

If the signs point toward termites instead, that is a different problem with a different fix, and we cover it in our pest and termite control in Tempe service.

Where Do Carpenter Bees Nest on Tempe Homes?

Carpenter bees go for dry, bare, softer wood. Painted and sealed surfaces are far less attractive to them. On Tempe homes the usual spots are:

  • Fascia boards and eaves, especially on the sunny south and west sides
  • Patio covers, ramadas and pergola beams
  • Unpainted fence rails and posts
  • Wooden gates, sheds and swing sets
  • Dead palm trunks and old agave flower stalks in the yard

Tempe has plenty of mid-century and 1980s-era homes where the wood trim has gone years between paint jobs, and Arizona sun dries and cracks that wood fast. Bare, weathered wood is exactly what a female is looking for.

Do Carpenter Bees Sting, and Are They Dangerous?

Males cannot sting at all. Females can, but they rarely do unless you grab one or trap it against your skin. A sting hurts, and anyone with a known bee allergy should treat any bee encounter seriously and get medical help for a reaction. Compared with Africanized honey bees, which defend a hive aggressively, carpenter bees are mostly a property problem, not a safety one.

The real damage comes from repetition. The same tunnel gets reused and lengthened year after year, and each new female adds galleries. Over several seasons that can weaken a fascia board or a pergola beam. Woodpeckers sometimes tear at the wood to reach the larvae, which makes the damage worse.

How Do You Get Rid of Wood-Boring Bees?

The reliable approach has four steps, and the order matters:

  1. Find every entrance. Walk the eaves, fascia, patio cover and fence line. Fresh sawdust tells you which holes are active.
  2. Treat the gallery. A labeled insecticide dust applied into each active hole reaches the female and the larvae inside. Always follow the product label and wear eye and hand protection.
  3. Wait, then plug. Do not seal a hole the same day. Wait until the adults and developing young are gone, then fill the hole with wood filler or dowel so a new female cannot move in.
  4. Finish the wood. Paint, stain or seal the surface. Bare wood invites bees, and a coated surface usually does not.

Sealing too early is the most common mistake we see. A plugged hole with live bees inside can send them chewing a new exit, sometimes through the interior side of the same board.

Do Home Remedies for Carpenter Bees Work?

Some help a little and most do not solve it. Here is what we tell Tempe homeowners:

  • Citrus or almond oil sprays. They may irritate bees for a day or two, but they do not reach the larvae deep in the tunnel.
  • Fake wasp nests. The evidence for them is weak. Carpenter bees are solitary and are not territorial about wasps.
  • Vibration and noise. Bees nesting in a quiet eave rarely care.
  • Traps. Wooden carpenter bee traps catch some adults, but they do not clear existing galleries.
  • Paint and stain. This is the one that works long term, as prevention after treatment.

When Should You Call a Professional?

Call when the nest is high, over a patio you use, in a structural beam, or when you cannot tell whether you have carpenter bees, honey bees or termites. Getting that identification wrong is the expensive part, because the treatment for each is different. A technician can identify the insect, treat the gallery safely and tell you whether any wood needs repair.

How Do You Keep Carpenter Bees From Coming Back?

Carpenter bees become active in the Valley as spring warms and stay busy through summer, so the cooler months are the time to get ahead of them. If you are reading this in the fall or winter, inspect your fascia and patio cover now and coat any bare wood before the next season.

  • Paint or seal all exposed wood, including the underside of eaves and the ends of beams.
  • Choose hardwood, vinyl or metal where you are rebuilding trim.
  • Fill old holes after the bees are gone so nothing re-nests in them.
  • Remove dead palm trunks and agave stalks you do not need.
  • Check the same spots every spring.

Frequently Asked Questions About Wood-Boring Bees in Tempe

What are wood-boring bees?

They are carpenter bees, large solitary bees that drill round tunnels in dry wood to nest. In Tempe, they most often use fascia boards, eaves, patio covers and fence rails.

Do wood-boring bees eat wood like termites?

No. Carpenter bees chew wood to make a tunnel but do not digest it. Termites eat the cellulose in wood, which is a separate and often more serious problem.

Can carpenter bees damage my house?

Yes, over time. One hole is minor, but tunnels reused and extended for several years can weaken trim and beams, and woodpeckers may tear at the wood to reach the larvae.

No. Treat the gallery first and wait until the adults and young are gone. Sealing too early can trap live bees, which may chew a new way out.

It helps a lot. They prefer bare, weathered wood, and a good coat of paint or stain makes it far less attractive.

what-is-a-pre-emergent-herbicide-what-ph.title: What Is a Pre-Emergent Herbicide? What Phoenix Homeowners Should Know
what-is-a-pre-emergent-herbicide-what-ph.excerpt: A pre-emergent herbicide stops weed seeds from sprouting; it does not kill weeds already up. Here is how it works in Phoenix, when to apply it and when to call us.
what-is-a-pre-emergent-herbicide-what-ph.content:
A pre-emergent herbicide is a weed-prevention product that forms a barrier in the top layer of soil and stops weed seeds from germinating, so weeds never break the surface. It does not kill weeds that are already growing. In Phoenix, that makes it the first step of any weed plan, followed by a post-emergent treatment for anything that slips through. If you want it done right, call us at (480) 422-8388 and we will set up pre-emergent weed control in Phoenix for your yard.

We hear this question from homeowners all over 85016, 85018, 85028, 85032, 85041 and 85054, from the gravel front yards near Arcadia and the Biltmore area to the newer desert-landscape lots around Desert Ridge. The pattern is almost always the same: a yard that looked clean in October is full of green by January, and the homeowner wonders why the weeds came back so fast after being pulled. The answer is that pulling a weed does nothing about the thousands of seeds already sitting in the soil, which is exactly the problem a pre-emergent is built to solve.

What Is a Pre-Emergent Herbicide and How Does It Work?

A pre-emergent herbicide is applied to bare soil or turf before weed seeds sprout. It sits in the top layer of soil and interrupts the seedling as it tries to germinate and root. The seed may still be there, but the weed never gets established. Think of it as a barrier you lay down ahead of the weeds, not a spray you use after they show up.

A few points about how it behaves:

  • It targets seeds, not plants. A weed that has already sprouted and rooted is mostly unaffected by a pre-emergent.
  • It needs to be watered in. Product has to move into the soil to form the barrier, so irrigation or rain after application matters.
  • It works for a limited window. The barrier breaks down over time. The commercial products we use are designed to hold for roughly three to four months per application.
  • It does not disturb the barrier if left alone. Raking, scalping or heavy digging breaks the treated layer and opens a path for seeds.

What Is the Difference Between Pre-Emergent and Post-Emergent Weed Control?

Pre-emergent stops weeds before they sprout, while post-emergent kills weeds that have already come up. Most Phoenix yards need both: pre-emergent to cut down how many weeds appear, and post-emergent to clean up the ones that get through. Using only one leaves a gap.

Does it affect existing weeds?Mostly noYes, that is the point

Which Weeds Does a Pre-Emergent Stop in Phoenix?

A pre-emergent works best on weeds that spread by seed. In the Phoenix area that includes the winter weeds that show up in fall and winter, such as London rocket and prickly lettuce, and the summer weeds that appear after the weather warms, such as spurge and puncture vine. It is much less effective on weeds that spread by roots, runners or rhizomes.

Bermuda grass in rock beds is the weed we see most often that a pre-emergent alone will not solve. If that is your problem, see how we approach it in our guide to Bermuda grass seeding and removal timing in Phoenix.

When Should You Apply a Pre-Emergent in Phoenix?

In Arizona, pre-emergents are applied before each weed season: in early fall to get ahead of winter weeds and in late winter to get ahead of summer weeds. The point is to treat before seeds sprout, because once the weeds are up, the barrier no longer helps with that crop.

If you are reading this in early November and weeds are already green in your rock, you are past the best window for the fall barrier. The practical move now is post-emergent control on what is up, followed by a pre-emergent in late winter so summer weeds do not get a head start.

Can You Use Pre-Emergent and Overseed the Same Lawn?

Usually not at the same time. A pre-emergent works by stopping seeds from sprouting, and that includes the ryegrass seed you spread for a winter lawn. If you plan to overseed in October, the pre-emergent timing has to be sequenced around it, or you can end up with a thin, patchy winter lawn.

Homeowners with Bermuda lawns who overseed face a real trade-off, which is why we plan the schedule rather than just applying product. Gravel and rock yards, which are never overseeded, can be treated on the normal fall and late-winter schedule. Our overseeding in Phoenix page explains how we handle winter lawns, and our guide to pre-emergent treatment near Desert Ridge covers the weed side of that decision.

Why Do Weeds Still Show Up After a Pre-Emergent?

Weeds can still appear after a pre-emergent because the barrier is never perfect. Common causes include missed timing, skipped watering, disturbed soil, wind-blown seeds landing on top of the barrier and weeds that spread by roots instead of seed. A few escapes do not mean the treatment failed.

  • Timing was late. If seeds had already germinated, the barrier cannot stop them.
  • The product was not watered in. Without moisture, it does not move into the soil to form a layer.
  • The soil was disturbed. Raking, digging or adding fresh rock breaks the treated layer.
  • Seeds blew in on top. Dust and organic debris on gravel can collect seeds that sprout in the debris itself.
  • It is a runner weed. Bermuda grass and some perennials spread underground and are not stopped by a seed barrier.

This is why we treat pre-emergent as one part of a program. Our guide to weed-free gravel yards in Phoenix shows how barrier, spot treatment and cleanup fit together in a rock yard.

Is Pre-Emergent Safe Around Kids, Pets and Plants?

Pre-emergent products are labeled for residential use, and the label is the final word on how long to stay off the area and how much to water. Follow the directions for your specific product. We tell customers what we applied, where, and when it is safe to be back on the lawn or in the yard.

Plants matter too. A pre-emergent near flower beds, new plantings or seeds you want to grow can stop those seeds as well. If you are planning to seed a bare patch, tell us before the application so we can leave that spot out.

Should You Apply Pre-Emergent Yourself or Hire a Professional?

DIY pre-emergent works for a small yard if you read the label, measure the area, time it correctly and water it in. A professional makes more sense for large or mixed yards, anything involving a lawn you plan to overseed, or when weeds keep returning despite your efforts. The product is only part of the job; timing and coverage drive the result.

  2. We time the barrier to the season. Early fall and late winter, adjusted for your lawn and overseeding plans.
  3. We cover the whole area evenly. Gaps in the barrier are where weeds break through.
  4. We follow up. Post-emergent spot treatment handles escapes between pre-emergent applications.

when-to-aerate-a-lawn-what-phoenix-homeo.title: When to Aerate a Lawn in Phoenix: What Bermuda Grass Homeowners Should Know
when-to-aerate-a-lawn-what-phoenix-homeo.excerpt: Aerate a Phoenix Bermuda lawn in late spring or early summer, when it is growing fast, not in winter. Here is the calendar, the weed trap and when to call us.
when-to-aerate-a-lawn-what-phoenix-homeo.content:
In Phoenix, the best time to aerate a Bermuda lawn is late spring through early summer, roughly May to June, when the grass is growing fast and can recover quickly. Do not aerate a dormant winter lawn, and do not do it right before or after a pre-emergent weed treatment without a plan. Aeration is the one lawn job where the weeds can win if the sequence is wrong, so if you want your schedule built around it, call us at (480) 422-8388 and we will map it into your weed and feed program in Phoenix.

We get this question from homeowners in 85016, 85018, 85028, 85032, 85044 and 85054, from the Arcadia and Biltmore lots with their older Bermuda lawns to the newer Desert Ridge and Ahwatukee yards where the soil was packed down by construction equipment. The advice you find online mostly comes from places with cool-season grass and a wet climate, where fall is the aeration season. That calendar is backwards for Phoenix, and following it is how people end up with scalped, stressed or weedy lawns.

When Is the Best Time to Aerate a Lawn in Phoenix?

The best time to aerate a Phoenix Bermuda lawn is when the grass is actively growing, from about May through June and into early summer. Warm soil and fast growth let the turf fill in the holes within a few weeks. Aerating in the cool months, when Bermuda is dormant or covered with a ryegrass overseed, stresses the lawn and gives weeds an opening.

Here is how the Phoenix year breaks down for aeration:
