If you are reading this in early November, you are in the "no" part of the calendar. The practical plan is to wait until spring, and use the winter months to get weeds under control. Our guide to timing Bermuda grass seeding and prep in Phoenix shows how the same warm-soil logic applies to seeding.

What Does Aerating a Lawn Actually Do?

Aeration pulls small plugs of soil out of the lawn, or pokes holes in it, so water, air and fertilizer reach the roots instead of running off or sitting on top. Core aeration, which removes plugs, is the version most turf guides recommend. It relieves compaction, which is the real problem it solves.

  • Water gets in. Compacted soil sheds water, so you see runoff and dry patches even when the sprinklers run.
  • Roots go deeper. Looser soil lets Bermuda roots grow down instead of staying shallow and burning in July.
  • Fertilizer works better. Nutrients move into the root zone instead of sitting on the surface.
  • Thatch breaks up. Plugs and the holes they leave help break up the buildup that blocks water.

Aeration does not kill weeds, fix irrigation problems or replace feeding. It is one step in a lawn schedule, not a cure for a thin lawn.

Does a Phoenix Lawn Need Aeration at All?

Many do. Valley soil tends to be alkaline and clay-heavy in places, with caliche, a hard mineral layer, sitting under the surface in many neighborhoods. New subdivisions are often built on soil compacted by heavy equipment, and the thin layer of topsoil the builder spreads over it can stay hard for years.

Signs your lawn is compacted:

  1. Water pools or runs off. Sprinklers finish and the water sits on the surface or runs into the street.
  2. A screwdriver will not push in. If you cannot push one in a few inches after watering, the soil is hard.
  3. Thin turf in high-traffic spots. Paths, play areas and dog runs thin out first.
  4. Weeds fill the bare spots. Compacted turf thins out and weed seeds move in.

If none of that sounds like your yard, you may not need to aerate. A lawn on healthy soil that drains well can skip it for a year or two.

Can You Aerate and Apply Pre-Emergent in the Same Season?

You can, but the order matters. A pre-emergent weed treatment forms a barrier in the top layer of soil, and aeration punches through that barrier. If you aerate right after a pre-emergent, you break the seal and weed seeds can sprout through the holes. The safer sequence is to aerate first, then apply the barrier.

This is the part most national articles skip, and it is where we spend our time with Phoenix customers. Here is how we think about the sequence:

OrderWhat happensResult
Aerate, then pre-emergentBarrier is laid over the finished soil surfaceBest for weed control
Pre-emergent, then aeratePlugs and holes break the barrierGaps where weeds sprout
Aerate and overseed in fallSeed lands in the holes, but pre-emergent cannot go down at the same timePick one: seed or barrier
Aerate, then wait a few weeks, then feedLawn recovers before fertilizer goes onEven regrowth

For the pre-emergent side, read our guide to what a pre-emergent herbicide is and how it works in Phoenix. For the seed side, our overseeding in Phoenix page explains the winter lawn schedule.

How Often Should You Aerate a Lawn in Arizona?

Most Phoenix lawns need aeration about once a year if the soil is compacted and every one to two years if it drains well. Heavily used lawns and yards built on hard-packed new-construction soil lean toward once a year. Do not aerate more often than your lawn can recover, because every pass opens the turf to weeds and stress.

  • New-construction lawns: often once a year for the first few years.
  • Older lawns with good soil: every one to two years or only when you see compaction signs.
  • Lawns with kids and pets: more often, because traffic compacts the soil.

Should You Aerate Before or After Overseeding?

If you aerate for overseeding, do it right before you spread seed, so the seed falls into the holes and contacts soil. But many Phoenix homeowners do not need to aerate at all for a winter ryegrass lawn, and the timing, October rather than May, is a different season entirely. We cover that decision in our guide to overseeding timing near Desert Ridge.

What Should You Do After Aerating a Phoenix Lawn?

Water the lawn right away, leave the plugs on the surface to break down, and hold off on mowing short or scalping. Feed the lawn a few weeks later once new growth appears, because Bermuda recovers fastest when it gets nutrients while it is actively growing. Our lawn fertilization in Phoenix service handles the feeding side, and our guide to lawn fertilization advice near Norterra explains what Phoenix Bermuda needs and when.

  1. Water within a day. It helps the plugs break down and the roots recover.
  2. Leave the plugs. They crumble back into the lawn in a couple of weeks.
  3. Skip heavy foot traffic. Give the turf time to close up.
  4. Fill in thin spots. Bermuda spreads by runners, so it usually closes the gaps on its own in warm weather.
  5. Check for weeds in two to three weeks. Fresh holes are where weeds get started.

signs-of-white-ants-in-a-phoenix-house-w.title: Signs of White Ants in a Phoenix House: Are They Termites?
signs-of-white-ants-in-a-phoenix-house-w.excerpt: White ants in a Phoenix house are almost always termites. Here are the signs, how to tell them from ants, and what to do next.
signs-of-white-ants-in-a-phoenix-house-w.content:
"White ants" in a Phoenix house are termites, not ants. Pale, soft-bodied insects in your walls, mud tubes on the foundation, or small piles of discarded wings near a window are the classic signs of subterranean termite activity. If you are seeing any of them, call us at (480) 422-8388 for an inspection through our termite treatment in Phoenix service.

We hear the phrase "white ants" from homeowners in 85016, 85018, 85024, 85028, 85032 and 85044, usually after they find something odd on a patio, in a garage or along a baseboard. The name is old-fashioned, but the worry behind it is real: termites are the one household pest that can quietly damage a structure for years before anyone sees it. This guide walks through what to look for, what is harmless, and what to do in the first 24 hours.

What Are White Ants, and Are They Really Termites?

"White ant" is a common name for termites. Termites are not ants at all. They belong to a different insect group, they live on wood and plant material, and they are pale and soft because they spend nearly their whole lives hidden inside soil, mud tubes and wood. In the Phoenix area the culprit is almost always the subterranean termite, which nests in the ground and travels up into the house.

Three body features separate a termite from an ant:

  • Waist: an ant has a pinched, narrow waist. A termite's body is thick and straight from chest to tail.
  • Antennae: ant antennae are bent like an elbow. Termite antennae are straight and bead-like.
  • Wings: a winged ant has a front pair of wings bigger than the back pair. A winged termite has four wings of about equal length, which break off easily.

What Are the Signs of White Ants in a House?

The most common signs of termites in a Phoenix home are mud tubes along the foundation or garage walls, swarmers and shed wings near windows and doors, hollow-sounding wood, and tiny pellets or blistered paint. Is a Flying White Insect in My House a Termite or a Flying Ant?

If the flying insect has a thick, straight body, straight antennae and four equal-length wings, it is a termite swarmer. A flying ant has a pinched waist, elbowed antennae and unequal wings. Swarming termites often drop their wings within minutes, so a pile of wings on a sill is the best clue after the swarm has passed.

Seeing swarmers outside near a tree stump or block wall is a warning, but seeing them inside your house is more urgent, because it suggests the colony is already in or under the structure. Save a few wings or a few insects in a sealed container or on a piece of clear tape. That gives a technician something to identify on the spot.

When Do White Ants Show Up in Phoenix?

Termite swarms in the Phoenix area are tied to moisture and warmth. Many homeowners notice them after monsoon storms from July through September, but swarms can also appear in spring and after heavy irrigation or a plumbing leak. Termite activity inside the walls does not follow the calendar, so the absence of a swarm does not mean a home is clear.

Here is how the seasons tend to look for Phoenix homeowners:

  • Spring: warming soil can bring the first swarms, especially after winter rain.
  • Summer monsoon: humidity and storms trigger the most reported swarms and shed wings.
  • Fall and winter: fewer swarms, but workers keep feeding in protected soil and walls, and mud tubes are easier to spot when you walk the foundation.

Why Are Phoenix Homes at Risk From Termites?

Phoenix is dry, but a house changes the soil around it. Irrigation lines, drip emitters, swamp coolers, planter beds against the stucco and roof run-off all create steady moisture next to the foundation, and subterranean termites follow moisture. Block and stucco construction also hides the slab edge, so a mud tube can run behind a stucco weep screed for a long way before it shows.

Older Phoenix neighborhoods such as Arcadia, Biltmore, Encanto and Maryvale have mature landscaping and wood trim that have had decades to settle against the soil. Newer areas in north Phoenix and Ahwatukee often have fresh fill dirt, new irrigation and raised planters that bring moisture close to the structure. Both kinds of home deserve a look.

What Is Harmless and What Is Not?

Not every pale insect is a termite. Here is a quick way to sort out the common look-alikes before you panic:

  • Flying ants: a nuisance, not wood eaters. They leave wings too, but with a pinched waist.
  • Carpenter ants and carpenter bees: they excavate wood but do not eat it, and they leave coarse sawdust or round holes. See our guide on wood-boring bees in eaves and patio covers.
  • Booklice and other pale pantry pests: tiny and pale, found in damp books or cupboards, not in walls.
  • Termites: straight body, straight antennae, mud tubes, hollow wood. These need treatment.

What Should I Do if I Find White Ants in My House?

Do not spray store-bought insecticide on the insects and do not knock down mud tubes yet. Spray can scatter the colony and make it harder to find where it enters. Instead, follow these steps in order:

  2. Save a few specimens in a sealed container.

How Can I Prevent Termites Around My Phoenix Home?

You cannot make a house termite-proof, but you can remove what draws termites close:

  • Keep irrigation heads and drip lines from spraying directly on stucco or the slab edge.
  • Fix leaking hose bibs, downspouts and cooler drains right away.
  • Keep wood, cardboard and firewood off the ground and away from the foundation.
  • Keep planter beds and mulch a few inches below the stucco weep screed line.
  • Walk your foundation twice a year and look for fresh mud tubes.

A yearly inspection is the single best habit, especially for homes that have never been treated or whose records you do not have.

Frequently Asked Questions About White Ants in Phoenix Homes

Are white ants the same as termites?

Yes. "White ant" is an old name for termites. They are not ants, and they eat wood and other plant material instead of food scraps.

What do white ants look like in a house?

Workers are small, pale and soft-bodied with a thick, straight body. Swarmers are darker, winged and have four wings of equal length that drop off after they land.

Can I tell if I have termites by seeing wings on my window sill?

Shed wings are a strong sign that a swarm happened nearby. It does not prove the colony is inside the house, so an inspection is the only way to know.

Do termites swarm in the Phoenix winter?

Swarms are most common in spring and during the summer monsoon, but hidden feeding continues year round. Check your foundation for mud tubes in any season.

Should I kill the white ants myself?

We advise against it. Over-the-counter sprays can scatter a colony and hide the entry points. Take photos, leave the evidence in place and call a licensed pest professional.
